name: GTR Curved Glass Tank Kit
summary: A curved-front glass tank sold as a full kit on a matching black cabinet, with a lid, LED lighting and a top filter box driven by a powerhead. Three footprints from 27 to 81 litres, all at the same 76 cm cabinet height.
highlights: Curved front glass on a matching cabinet
Lid with white and blue LEDs on a 3-way touch switch
Top filter box and powerhead included
bestFor: Someone who wants a complete tank-and-stand package for a low-tech planted community tank without piecing parts together.
watchOut: The curved front bends the view slightly and is awkward to scrape, and the included lid light and top filter are basic, so a serious planted tank will need upgrades.

specs.Included: Cabinet, lid, white/blue LED light, top filter box with powerhead

name: GT3000 Series Glass Tank
summary: Plain frameless glass tanks in five sizes from about 15 to 57 litres, offered with either bent-glass round front corners or square corners with black silicone. They are sold bare, which is exactly what many scapers want as a starting point.
highlights: Five sizes from 30 to 50 cm long
4 mm glass on the two smallest, 5 mm on the rest
Nested value sets of 3 or 5 tanks available
bestFor: A budget nano or small scape where you plan to choose your own light, filter and CO2.
watchOut: Glass is on the thin side for the 45 and 50 cm sizes, so sit them on a levelling mat on a flat, solid surface; no lid, light or filter is included.

specs.Corners: Round (bent glass) or square with black silicone

name: GT6000 Cube Glass Tank
summary: A 25 cm glass cube in two heights, 15 and 18 litres, with silver or black silicone. It is a simple, cheap way into a nano cube scape.
highlights: 25 x 25 cm footprint, 25 or 30 cm tall
bestFor: A shrimp or nano cube with mosses, small epiphytes and a carpet, where the taller GT-6002 gives a little more room for stem plants.
watchOut: Cubes this small swing in temperature and water chemistry quickly, so they need steady maintenance.

name: BT Mini Tank
summary: Two tiny desktop all-in-ones of about 5 litres, one squared off (BT-111) and one round (BT-112). Each has a small internal filter with a replaceable cartridge and a 2 W white LED running off a 12 V transformer.
highlights: Around 5 litres, built for desks and shelves
bestFor: A moss, Anubias or shrimp display on a desk where you want everything in one box.
watchOut: At around 5 litres this is too small for most fish, a betta included, and the light is only good for low-light plants.

name: CF11008 Series CO2 Canister Filter
summary: A squared-off canister with two planted-tank extras built in: a CO2 inlet that mixes gas from your cylinder into the filter flow, and a bay that holds a standard glass heater inside the head. Three sizes rated 950 to 1450 L/h.
highlights: CO2 inlet and mixing chamber in the filter, cylinder not included
Internal bay for a 22 to 24 mm heater keeps the tank clear of kit
bestFor: A budget planted tank of roughly 60 to 140 litres where you want CO2 and heating hidden inside the filter.
watchOut: The maker warns to turn the CO2 off before unplugging, or water can back up out of the CO2 tube; as with any filter-mixed CO2, some gas can collect in the canister.

specs.CO2: Built-in inlet and mixing system; connect your own cylinder and regulator
specs.Heater bay: Takes a 22 to 24 mm diameter heater (not included)

name: CF688 Series Canister Filter
summary: A round blue canister range from 800 to 1400 L/h, each size available with or without a built-in UV lamp (the UV versions add a UV suffix). On those, the lamp sits in a quartz sleeve inside the canister.
highlights: Optional internal UV lamp of 5 to 9 W
Spray bar, inlet and outlet pipes and a directional spout included
bestFor: A 60 to 140 litre tank that suffers green water now and then, where a UV option in the same box saves buying a separate unit.
watchOut: UV only kills free-floating algae and microbes, not algae on leaves, and running it constantly can break down some chelated trace elements, so many planted-tank keepers only switch it on when needed.

specs.UV: Optional; UV models are CF688UV, CF888UV, CF1288UV, CF1488UV (uvW applies to these)

name: CF Series UV Canister Filter
summary: A grey canister range from a 410 L/h mini up to the big 3000 L/h C2400, with most sizes offered with an internal UV lamp. The CF1200 and CF1400 share their ratings with the CF1288 and CF1488 in a different body.
highlights: UV lamp of 5 to 9 W on UV versions
CF300 mini canister for small tanks
bestFor: Anyone wanting a cheap canister with optional UV, from a 40 litre shrimp tank (CF300) to a large display (C2400).
watchOut: UV does nothing for algae growing on plants and can reduce some chelated trace elements if left on all the time; the C2400 is a big unit that needs cabinet space.

specs.UV: Optional on CF600 to C2400 (UV suffix models); CF300 has no UV

name: C Series Canister Filter
summary: A tall, square brown canister line from C-500 to C-1600 with a push-button primer and double valve taps. The number of media baskets grows from two to five as you go up the range.
highlights: Push-button primer and double shut-off taps
Spray bar and intake strainer included
bestFor: A 100 to 190 litre planted tank on a budget where you want room for plenty of your own media.
watchOut: The flow ratings are for the bare pump; packed with media and hoses the real flow is well below that, though still generous for the listed tank sizes.

specs.Media supplied: Carbon, quartz rings, black sponge, white wool (varies by size)

name: CF2000 Pre-Canister Filter
summary: A small canister that sits in the intake line before your main filter and catches the muck first. It has its own media holder and a drain valve, so you empty the pre-filter often and open the main canister far less.
highlights: Traps debris before it reaches the main canister
bestFor: A planted tank with lots of leaf litter or trimmings where you are tired of stripping down the main canister.
watchOut: It has no pump of its own, adds another hose run and some flow resistance, and must be kept clean or it will choke the main filter's flow.

specs.Pump: None, runs on your main canister's flow

name: Power Head Top Filter
summary: A long plastic filter tray that sits across the top of the tank, fed by a submersible powerhead. Four lengths fit tanks from about 47 cm up to 127 cm.
highlights: Tray lengths to suit 47 to 127 cm tanks
bestFor: An older-style framed tank without a lid where you want a lot of cheap, easy-to-clean media.
watchOut: A top filter blocks part of the tank top, clashing with most planted-tank lights, and its trickle return drives off CO2.

name: FC Filter Box
summary: Slim box-shaped internal filters with the pump at the bottom and a waterfall-style outlet at the top. Most use a drop-in sponge and carbon cartridge, and the range runs from tiny nano sizes up to the tall FC-601.
highlights: Low-mounted pump pulls from near the substrate
Drop-in cartridge, so no wet hands
bestFor: A small desktop or nano tank that needs a compact, cheap internal filter.
watchOut: Cartridges are an ongoing cost, and the waterfall outlet splashes, which is poor for CO2; for planted tanks swap the carbon for plain sponge once it is spent.

specs.Media: Sponge and carbon cartridge (FC-601 uses layered media)

name: SH Slim Hanging Filter
summary: A slim hang-on-back filter only 5 cm deep, with the motor down on the intake tube and a floating surface skimmer built into the intake. Sizes differ mainly in how many standard carbon cartridges they hold.
highlights: Only 5 cm deep behind the tank
Built-in floating surface skimmer clears surface film
bestFor: A 20 to 80 litre tank with a lid-free top where you want surface film gone without a separate skimmer.
watchOut: The cartridges contain carbon, which you may prefer to replace with sponge in a fertilised planted tank, and the spill-over outlet gasses off some CO2.

specs.Cartridges: One standard size across the range

name: A Series Hanging Filter
summary: A chunky hang-on-back filter with adjustable flow, an extendable intake and a media-change reminder dial. It comes either with an open media box (sponge, carbon, bio balls) or a carbon cartridge.
highlights: Choice of open media box or carbon cartridge version
bestFor: A 40 to 100 litre tank where you want a simple hang-on filter you can fill with your own media.
watchOut: Get the media box version for a planted tank, so you can skip carbon; like all hang-on filters the waterfall return drives off some CO2.

specs.Versions: Media box (sponge, carbon, bio balls) or carbon cartridge

name: H Series Hanging Filter
summary: A classic smoked-grey hang-on-back range from the tiny H-80 to the 1000 L/h H-800. Each uses a bio cartridge plus a carbon cartridge that needs changing periodically.
bestFor: A beginner tank from 25 to 200 litres where a familiar, easy hang-on filter is enough.
watchOut: The carbon cartridge is a running cost and strips some liquid fertiliser, so planted-tank keepers often swap it for sponge.

name: TF Internal Filter
summary: A tall corner-style internal filter that comes with a spray bar, so the return can be spread along the back of the tank instead of blasting one spot.
highlights: Slim profile for the back corner
bestFor: A 50 to 150 litre tank where you want gentle, spread-out flow without a canister.
watchOut: Internal filters take up visible space in the scape, and the media capacity is small next to a canister.

name: KF Internal Filter
summary: Very small internal filters, only 8 to 9.5 cm tall, with an adjustable outlet nozzle. The KF-160 is a taller take on the KF-150, rated for tanks up to 30 litres.
bestFor: A nano or shrimp tank of 30 to 70 litres that needs a tiny, cheap internal filter.
watchOut: The intake is not shrimp-safe as supplied, so cover it with a sponge in a breeding tank.

name: FB Internal Filter
summary: A plain rectangular internal filter with a sponge body and a side outlet that can take a rain bar. Four sizes cover roughly 50 to 140 litres.
highlights: Rain bar option for spread flow
bestFor: A basic community or planted tank where a simple sponge internal filter is enough.
watchOut: Media volume is small, so it needs rinsing often in a heavily stocked tank.

name: 950F Series Internal Filter
summary: A powerhead sitting on top of a slotted strainer tube packed with sponge. The bigger 970F and 980F push a lot of water for an internal filter.
bestFor: A larger tank that needs strong extra circulation plus some mechanical filtration.
watchOut: The larger sizes are bulky and strong for a planted tank; they can flatten stem plants and are hard to hide.

name: F Series Internal Filter
summary: A tall, slim internal filter in three sizes with a blue flow-adjust knob on top; the small F-800 can take a rain bar.
bestFor: A mid-sized tank where you want an internal filter that tucks into a back corner.
watchOut: Like any internal box it takes up room in the scape and holds less media than a canister.

name: PC Series Submersible Pump
summary: Compact square submersible pumps from 300 to 5000 L/h. The three largest get a carry handle and a flow controller.
highlights: Up to 3 m head on the largest
Flow controller on PC-3000, PC-4000, PC-5000
bestFor: A return pump for a sump, a DIY filter or water changes, sized to your head height.
watchOut: Watts climb steeply on the bigger models (120 W for the PC-5000), so check running cost if it will run all day.

name: P Series Submersible Pump
summary: A long-running range of grey and black submersible pumps from 320 to 3000 L/h with a blue flow dial on the smaller models.
highlights: Flow adjustment dial on small and mid sizes
bestFor: Driving a DIY filter, a sump return or a water-change setup on a budget.
watchOut: The large models draw 66 to 88 W, which is a lot for a pump running around the clock.

name: PH Series Submersible Pump
summary: Small black submersible pumps from 300 to 1250 L/h, the sort used to drive a small DIY filter, a spray bar or water changes.
bestFor: Driving a DIY sponge or box filter, adding a little extra flow, or topping up from a bucket.
watchOut: Head figures are the maximum lift with zero flow, so size up if you need to push water more than a metre.

name: AA Series Submersible Pump
summary: Grey and blue submersible pumps with a carry handle on the bigger sizes, running from 300 to 4300 L/h. Sold as "power liquid filter" pumps, they are general-purpose water movers.
highlights: Up to 4 m head on the AA9000
bestFor: A sump return or water-transfer pump where you need decent head height for the money.
watchOut: Power draw is high on the big models (116 to 125 W for AA6000 and AA9000); an efficient DC pump costs more upfront but less to run.

name: ECO DC Variable Pump
summary: A 24 V DC pump with a digital remote that gives 20 steps of steady flow, two wave modes and a feed pause. It also cuts out and alarms if it runs dry.
highlights: 20-step flow control plus fast and slow wave modes
bestFor: A sump return on a large tank where turning the flow down precisely matters more than raw price.
watchOut: Even at its lowest setting it is a big pump, sized for large systems rather than a normal planted tank.

specs.Motor: 24 V DC, accepts 100 to 240 V AC input

name: WP Wave Pump
summary: A compact circulation pump on a suction-cup mount that tilts 100 degrees and swivels 360. Two sizes, rated 2000 and 5000 L/h.
bestFor: Adding gentle circulation to a larger planted tank to move CO2 and nutrients into dead spots.
watchOut: It gives steady flow only, no wave controller, and the WP-3000 can be too strong for tanks under about 200 litres.

specs.Mount: Suction cup, 100 degree tilt, 360 degree rotation

name: P-608 / P-908 Power Head
summary: A classic square aquarium powerhead, the same pump used on Dophin top filters. Fitted with its sponge it doubles as a basic internal filter.
highlights: Can run a top filter or undergravel setup
Sponge attachment shown on the box
bestFor: Driving a top filter or giving an old-school tank extra flow.
watchOut: At 16 to 29 W these are thirsty next to modern DC circulation pumps.

name: AP2500 Air Pump
summary: A tiny single-outlet air pump drawing just 1.2 W. Fine for a sponge filter or an air stone in a small tank.
bestFor: Running a sponge filter in a shrimp or nano tank.
watchOut: Output is modest, so it struggles with deeper tanks or more than one air device.

name: AP1500 Air Pump
summary: A low, compact single-outlet air pump putting out 0.6 L/min for under 2 W.
bestFor: A single small sponge filter or air stone in a nano tank.
watchOut: Low pressure (0.008 MPa), so keep it to shallow tanks.

name: AP1301 / AP1302 Air Pump
summary: A white, drum-shaped air pump in single (AP1301) and double outlet (AP1302) versions.
bestFor: Running one or two sponge filters in small to medium tanks.
watchOut: The double outlet splits a modest 2 L/min, so two devices each get only about 1 L/min.

name: AP1501 / AP1502 Air Pump
summary: A dome-shaped air pump with an adjustable air-flow dial on top, in single and double outlet versions. Ratings match the AP1301/AP1302.
bestFor: A sponge filter in a shrimp tank where you want to turn the bubbles down.
watchOut: Tubing and check valve are optional extras, and output is modest for deeper tanks.

name: FISH-1 / FISH-2 Air Pump
summary: A fish-shaped novelty air pump in two sizes, putting out 1 or 2.4 L/min.
bestFor: A simple aeration or sponge-filter pump where the look appeals.
watchOut: The shape is a matter of taste; performance is ordinary budget-pump level.

name: BP-1 Battery Air Pump
summary: A portable 1.5 V battery air pump in a blue case, supplied with tubing and an air stone. It is for transport and emergencies rather than daily use.
bestFor: Keeping fish or shrimp oxygenated in a bag or bucket on the way home, or during a power cut.
watchOut: Output is very low and it does not switch on by itself when the power fails.

name: BP-189 AC/DC Air Pump
summary: A small mains air pump with battery backup, so the air keeps running if the power cuts out. Output is 0.5 L/min.
highlights: AC mains with DC battery backup
bestFor: Keeping a sponge filter running through short power cuts in a small tank.
watchOut: Only 0.3 m maximum depth, so it will not push air to the bottom of tall tanks.

name: BP-188 AC/DC Air Pump
summary: A rescue air pump with a rechargeable 6 V 4.0 Ah battery. It switches to battery by itself when the mains fails and recharges once power returns.
highlights: Automatic switch to battery on power failure
bestFor: Anyone in an area with regular power cuts who wants filters and livestock kept oxygenated.
watchOut: It is bulky (18 x 16.5 x 7.7 cm) and the sealed battery will need replacing eventually.

specs.Battery: 6 V 4.0 Ah rechargeable, or 4 dry cells

name: AH-1010 Mini Heater
summary: A tiny quartz heater with a switch for 23, 25 or 27 °C. The three wattages each suit a nano of 5, 10 or 15 litres.
bestFor: A small shrimp or betta tank where you just want a stable, sensible temperature.
watchOut: No fine control between the three settings, so check with a thermometer.

name: AH-1000 Plastic Mini Heater
summary: A fully submersible plastic-cased mini heater preset to 25 °C, in 10 and 25 W sizes.
bestFor: A nano or small shrimp tank that just needs taking off the chill.
watchOut: No adjustment, so it will not suit fish that want cooler or warmer water; unplug before lifting it out.

name: AH-1008 Glass Heater
summary: A standard glass thermostat heater from 25 to 500 W, rated at roughly one watt per litre.
bestFor: A budget heater for a tropical planted tank, sized to your volume.
watchOut: Budget glass heaters can drift, so keep a thermometer in the tank and never run it out of water.

name: AH-1006 Glass Heater
summary: A glass thermostat heater with a printed temperature scale and a perforated lower sleeve, in the same 25 to 500 W steps as the AH-1008.
highlights: Printed temperature scale on the tube
bestFor: A tropical tank where you want a cheap heater with a visible scale.
watchOut: Treat the scale as a guide and confirm with a separate thermometer.

name: LED 109 Clip Light
summary: A slim 3.4 W clip-on LED with 12 white and 3 blue diodes on an arched arm. It clamps to glass up to 5 mm thick.
bestFor: A small nano with low-light plants such as Anubias, Bucephalandra, Java fern and mosses.
watchOut: Too weak for carpeting plants or red stems; treat it as a viewing light that keeps easy plants ticking over.

name: Mini LED Clip Light
summary: Small clip-on lights for tiny tanks: a gooseneck 8-LED spot and flat 10, 14 and 20 LED panels on a swivel clamp.
bestFor: Lighting a desktop tank or betta setup with a few low-light plants.
watchOut: Wattage and spectrum are not published; expect only enough light for the hardiest plants.

specs.Mount: Clip-on (gooseneck on 8 LED, swivel clamp on the others)

name: SK200 Surface Skimmer
summary: A small self-powered surface skimmer with its own 3 W pump. It pulls the oily film off the surface and returns the water, improving gas exchange.
bestFor: A small planted tank with a surface film problem that has no skimmer on the filter intake.
watchOut: At 200 L/h it is sized for small tanks, and the surface agitation it creates will drive off some CO2.
